answer.rationale: The binding constraint is timing and fragility, not information: the contract lapses in 14 days, the line is at 94% of committed volume with zero buffer, and I get one action. That rules out switch_primary_vendor (memory_c2 is explicit that the low-cost vendor missed SLA in three of four quarters and should not be sole source on a critical line — cheap unit cost bought with delivery risk directly violates the stated objective) and rules out defer_decision (memory_c5's deferral worked only because the service was non-critical and continued month-to-month; here there is no auto-renew and no slack, so drifting past expiry is an uncovered exposure, not flexibility). add_second_source is the right structural answer to concentration risk (memory_c3) but it does not deliver an 18% spend cut and cannot be stood up and qualified inside 14 days while the line runs with no buffer; it is the correct next-cycle action. Plain renew_incumbent (memory_c1) protects delivery but leaves the finance mandate wholly unmet. Negotiating at renewal is the one move that attacks cost without touching the physical supply path: memory_c4 says benchmarking moved the incumbent on both price and terms, and memory_c6 says term length unlocked volume pricing without narrowing scope. I am verifying exactly those two because they are the load-bearing claims and the ones most likely to be overstated in consolidation — I need the original records to see the actual magnitude recovered in c4 (is it plausibly near 18%, or 3%?), whether the benchmark leverage came from a credible alternative that still exists today, and in c6 what the multi-year commitment cost in flexibility and what volume floor it assumed. Both were consolidated from archived sources and stripped of numbers, which is precisely where inherited memory tends to flatter past decisions. Two risks I am holding open rather than resolving: negotiation may close only part of the 18% gap, in which case the residual has to come from scope, mix, or next-cycle dual-sourcing rather than from squeezing delivery; and a long-term lock-in signed under budget pressure at 94% utilization could foreclose the second-source move that memory_c3 shows actually protects allocation, and could bind us to a volume floor we cannot hold if demand softens. So I intend to negotiate for near-term price and payment-term relief while explicitly preserving the right to add a qualified second source, and I will resist trading term length for discount until the c6 record shows what that trade actually cost. If verification shows c4's recovery was marginal or its leverage came from a benchmark that no longer holds, I fall back to a short renewal that buys time to dual-source rather than chasing the cut through a risky vendor switch.
